title: Chapter 12 — How The Americans Understand The Equality Of The Sexes
paragraphs: I have shown how democracy destroys or modifies the various inequalities that originate in society. But is that all? Does it not in the end also affect that great inequality of man and woman which, until now, has seemed eternally rooted in human nature? I believe the social changes that bring father and son, master and servant, superiors and inferiors closer to the same level will also raise woman and make her more and more the equal of man. But here, more than anywhere, I feel the need to make myself clearly understood, for there is no subject on which the coarse and lawless fancies of our age have ranged more freely.

There are people in Europe who, confusing the distinct characters of the sexes, would make man and woman beings not only equal but identical. They would give both the same functions, impose on both the same duties, and grant both the same rights. They would mix them in everything — occupations, pleasures, business. One can easily imagine that by thus trying to make one sex the equal of the other, both are degraded. From such a preposterous jumbling of nature's work nothing could ever come but weak men and disorderly women. This is not how the Americans understand the kind of democratic equality that can be established between the sexes. They grant that, since nature has placed such wide differences between the physical and moral constitution of man and woman, her evident design was to give distinct work to their different faculties. They hold that improvement does not consist in making beings so unlike do nearly the same things, but in having each perform its respective tasks as well as possible. The Americans have applied to the sexes the great principle of political economy that governs the manufacturing of our age, carefully dividing the duties of man from those of woman so that the great work of society may be carried on all the better.

In no country has such constant care been taken as in America to trace two clearly distinct lines of action for the two sexes, and to make them keep pace with each other along two paths that are always different. American women never manage the outward concerns of the family, or conduct a business, or take part in political life. Nor are they, on the other hand, ever compelled to perform the rough labor of the fields or any of those heavy tasks that call for physical strength. No families are poor enough to form an exception to this rule. If on the one hand an American woman cannot escape the quiet circle of domestic employments, on the other hand she is never forced to go beyond it. That is why the women of America, who often display a masculine strength of understanding and a manly energy, generally preserve great delicacy of appearance and always retain the manners of women, even though they sometimes show they have the hearts and minds of men.

Nor have the Americans ever supposed that one consequence of democratic principles would be the overthrow of marital authority and the confusion of the natural authorities within families. They hold that every association must have a head in order to accomplish its purpose, and that the natural head of the conjugal association is man. They do not, therefore, deny him the right to guide his partner. They maintain that, in the small association of husband and wife, as in the great society at large, the purpose of democracy is to regulate and legitimize necessary powers, not to overturn all power. This opinion is not held by one sex and contested by the other. I never observed that the women of America regard marital authority as a lucky usurpation of their rights, or that they thought themselves degraded by submitting to it. On the contrary, it seemed to me that they take a kind of pride in the voluntary surrender of their own will, and that they boast of bending themselves to the yoke rather than shaking it off. Such at least is the feeling expressed by the most virtuous of their sex; the others are silent. And in the United States it is not the practice for a guilty wife to clamor for women's rights while trampling on her most sacred duties.

It has often been remarked that in Europe a certain contempt lurks even in the flattery men lavish on women. Although a European often pretends to be the slave of woman, it is clear that he never sincerely regards her as his equal. In the United States men seldom compliment women, but they show every day how much they esteem them. They constantly display complete confidence in a wife's understanding and a deep respect for her freedom. They have decided that her mind is just as fit as a man's to discover plain truth, and her heart as firm to embrace it. They have never tried to place her virtue, any more than his, under the shelter of prejudice, ignorance, and fear. It seems that in Europe, where man so easily submits to the despotic sway of women, women are nevertheless deprived of some of the greatest qualities of the human species and regarded as alluring but imperfect beings. And — what may well be astonishing — women in the end look on themselves in the same light and almost regard it as a privilege that they are entitled to show themselves frivolous, feeble, and timid. American women claim no such privileges.

Again, it may be said that in our morals we have reserved strange exemptions for man, so that there is, as it were, one virtue for his use and another for the guidance of his partner; and that in public opinion the very same act may be punished either as a crime or merely as a fault. The Americans know nothing of this unjust division of duties and rights. Among them the seducer is as dishonored as his victim. It is true that Americans rarely lavish on women the eager attentions commonly paid them in Europe. But their conduct toward women always implies that they take them to be virtuous and refined. So great is their respect for the moral freedom of the sex that in the presence of a woman the most guarded language is used, lest her ear be offended by an expression. In America a young unmarried woman can travel alone and without fear on a long journey.

The legislators of the United States, who have softened almost every penalty of the criminal law, still make rape a capital offense, and no crime is met with more unbending severity by public opinion. This can be explained. Since the Americans can imagine nothing more precious than a woman's honor, and nothing more deserving of respect than her independence, they hold that no punishment is too severe for a man who strips her of both against her will. In France, where the same offense is met with far milder penalties, it is often hard to get a verdict from a jury against the accused. Is this a consequence of contempt for decency or contempt for women? I cannot help believing that it is contempt for both.

The Americans, then, do not think that man and woman have either the duty or the right to perform the same offices. But they show equal regard for both their respective parts, and although their lot differs, they consider them both as beings of equal worth. They do not give to woman's courage the same form or direction as to man's, but they never doubt her courage. And if they hold that a man and his partner ought not always to use their intellect and understanding in the same way, they at least believe the understanding of the one to be as sound as that of the other, and her intellect as clear. Thus, while they have allowed the social inferiority of woman to continue, they have done everything they could to raise her morally and intellectually to the level of man. In this respect they seem to me to have grasped the true principle of democratic improvement admirably. As for myself, I do not hesitate to say that, although the women of the United States are confined within the narrow circle of domestic life and their situation is in some respects one of extreme dependence, I have nowhere seen woman holding a loftier position. And if I were asked, now that I am drawing to the close of this work in which I have spoken of so many important things done by the Americans, to what the singular prosperity and growing strength of that people should chiefly be attributed, I would reply: to the superiority of their women.
